title: Pongal / Onam (regional; harvest)
hook: a new clay pot of rice and milk set in the sun, and a whole family waiting for it to boil over
carry: more than the pot can hold

segments.voice: Yesterday, Makar Sankranti from the kitchen: sesame and sweet words, a cold river, a gift given freely. Your line was something sweet, something clean, something given. Today, Tamil Nadu, and a pot meant to overflow.

Milk on a stove rises, foams and spills over the side, and the cook lunges for the knob too late. In a kitchen, that's a small disaster. In a courtyard in Tamil Nadu in the middle of January, it's the whole point. A brand-new clay pot, a turmeric plant tied around its neck, sits on a little fire in the open sun. Rice, milk and jaggery inside. The whole family stands around it. They're waiting for it to boil over. And when it does, they shout.
screen: `THE MILK BOILS OVER.` → `A NEW CLAY POT IN THE SUN.` → `WAITING FOR IT TO SPILL.`

segments.voice: They shout Pongalo Pongal! Pongal means boiling over. It's the name of the dish, the sweet rice, and of the festival, Tamil Nadu's great harvest festival, in the Tamil month of Thai, on the same days as Makar Sankranti. The rice has just come in from the fields. The overflowing pot is abundance you can see: more than the pot can hold. Pongal runs four days, and each has a job. Day one, Bhogi: clear out the old. Families clean the house, and in many places old things go on a bonfire at dawn. Day two, Thai Pongal, the big day. A kolam, a pattern drawn in rice flour, is laid at the door. The pot boils over in the sun, and the first pongal is offered to Surya, the sun, before anyone eats. Day three, Mattu Pongal, for the cattle. The cows and bulls who plowed the fields are bathed, their horns painted, bells and garlands put on them, and they're fed pongal too: a whole day to thank the animals who did the work. Day four, Kaanum Pongal, for visiting family and friends, and outings. A Tamil saying for this week: Thai piranthal vazhi pirakkum. When Thai is born, a way will be born. A new month, and a new road opens. A harvest festival, and a very complete way of saying thank you.
screen: `PONGAL MEANS BOILING OVER.` · `BHOGI: CLEAR OUT THE OLD.` · `THE SUN, THEN THE CATTLE.` · `WHEN THAI IS BORN, A WAY IS BORN.` · then, large: `MORE THAN THE POT CAN HOLD.`

segments.voice: Walk through the four days in your mind: one old thing you're ready to put on the fire, a habit, a grudge, a drawer of junk, and one thing that simply gave you life this week, like light, food or sleep. Then silently thank someone who does the hard work so you can eat, earn or rest and rarely hears it, and name one person you'd like to go and see. Sit with the pot of your life, boiling over a little.
Pongal and Onam, two harvests. Today, Pongal: boiling over. Tamil Nadu's four-day harvest festival, when the new rice spills out of a new pot, and everyone says thank you.
Your line: more than the pot can hold. The overflow is the blessing. Day one hundred fifty-three, done.

howItsDone: Over four days in the Tamil month of Thai, many Tamil Hindus clear out old things on Bhogi, boil new rice with milk and jaggery until it overflows and offer it to the sun on Thai Pongal, honor their cattle on Mattu Pongal, and visit family on Kaanum Pongal.

notes: Pongal falls on the first of Thai (about January 14–15), overlapping Makar Sankranti. Confirm.
Bhogi bonfire of old items: common, now discouraged in cities for air quality. Confirm framing 'in many places'.
Turmeric plant tied around the pot; offering to Surya; kolam in rice flour. Confirm.
Kaanum Pongal described as visiting; also called Kanu Pongal in some families, with a rite for brothers. Confirm.
The original is given in Tamil script, since Pongal is a Tamil word. Confirm this is right for the Hindu path.
